newsitem.title: USA: Air control said worst in N.Y., Chicago, Ft. Worth.
newsitem.headline: Air control said worst in N.Y., Chicago, Ft. Worth.

text.p: Air traffic control centers in New York, Chicago and Fort Worth, Texas, guiding aircraft at high altitudes had the worst equipment failure records in the nation during the last 16 months, according to a study released on Tuesday.

Federal Aviation Administration data analyzed by the American Automobile Association showed 30 major computer and power failures at U.S. "en route" air traffic control centers during that time. New York, Chicago and Fort Worth accounted for 21 of these failures.
En route air traffic control centers control aircraft traveling at high altitudes between cities.

"These equipment failures are a prime example of the general deterioration of our transportation system," AAA President Robert Darbelnet said. "This is not a people problem. It is a hardware and under-investment problem."

The association said New York had eight incidents, including one that lasted nearly six hours and affected 485 flights. Chicago had seven, including a computer outage of 46 minutes that led to 313 flight delays. And Fort Worth had six major air traffic control failures, including a 14-hour power failure that resulted in 263 flight delays.
Those delays do not include hundreds of others "downline" caused by the ripple effect of the delayed aircraft arriving late at subsequent stops.
The FAA has estimated that on an average day there are 700 flight delays of 15 minutes or more, with an annual cost to airlines and their customers estimated at $3 billion.
The AAA undertook the study as part of a campaign to bring public attention to what it termed the "rapidly deteriorating" state of U.S. highways and the air traffic control system.
The AAA has 938 U.S. travel agency offices that sell more than $1 billion worth of air travel annually. It called on Congress to take immediate steps to help fix the air traffic control system.
In a statement, the FAA said "the reliability of the U.S. air traffic control system is 99.4 percent" and fewer than 3 percent of all delays were due to equipment problems.
The agency had undertaken an aggressive plan to maintain and enhance reliability, but faced a critical funding shortage, the statement said.

Without financial reform, the FAA said it would be unable to make the investments needed to meet the expected 35 percent increase in passengers by the year 2002, a funding shortfall that would "affect the safety and efficiency of the system."
